title: Best Schedule to Utilize the Big Long River

section_map.summary: The Introduction frames river popularity, wilderness separation, a 225-mile corridor, six-month scheduling, and three progressively less controlled schedule designs whose capacity and flexibility must be traded by managers.
The definitions assign operational meanings to optimal, route, orbit, twenty-six nominal trip types, daily travel demand, orbit size, and seasonal trip count.
The formulation represents the river as an ordered line of campsites and separates deterministic fixed-route, random-route, and random-type scheduling questions.
The assumptions impose downstream travel, one-night stops, a daily travel limit, uniform complete-route choice, a small-probability collision convention, and a worked value Y=150.
Part 1 motivates the most controlled schedule, defines exclusive campsite orbits, and decomposes the task into single-type, multi-type, and two-orbit regimes as Y decreases.
The single-type construction partitions campsites by residue, chooses a leader route, fills campsites ahead of the leader, repeats a short cycle, and maps requested type proportions to orbit sizes.
The multi-type construction shares each orbit among paired propulsion-compatible durations, derives a Y=150 two-day cycle, lists fixed routes, and reports 2,340 launches.
The orbit idea is extended from three durations to an arbitrary group and finally to one orbit per propulsion class for small Y.
Part 2 replaces fixed routes by an equal-probability route model, defines route-count, occupancy, and collision quantities, invokes inclusion-exclusion, and announces a greedy minimax schedule.
The paper recursively counts route prefixes and combines them with a printed suffix factor to estimate the probability that trip type T occupies campsite x on day t.

For each launch day the algorithm evaluates every candidate type, chooses the one minimizing the worst campsite-day collision probability, stops when the threshold fails, and displays a 180-day calendar totaling 500 trips.
Two continuation cases treat X given trips with free or fixed routes as an initial schedule state before the same probability-based construction continues.
Part 3 selects uniformly from currently feasible trip types rather than the greedy minimizer, reports eight capacities, and aggregates the resulting type frequencies.
Sensitivity tables vary the first trip type, daily travel hours, and the small-probability threshold, then interpret the resulting capacity changes.
The evaluation lists operational strengths, distributional weaknesses, and survey-based extensions for route and type-choice probabilities.
The conclusion restates the three control regimes, orbit, recursion, inclusion-exclusion, greedy and random mechanisms, and the headline capacities 2,340, 500, and 493.
Four web references provide weak practical context, including one duplicated source and no executable or archival reproduction package.
The manager letter translates the three schedules into choices between capacity and tourist freedom, repeats the headline figures, and delegates the final commercial and management decision.

assumptions.summary: The 225-mile river contains Y approximately uniform campsites and a six-month 180-day launch season.
Oar and motor craft average four and eight miles per hour and nominal durations span six through eighteen days.
Travel proceeds only downstream, each campsite is used for one night, and a new campsite is reached every day.
Travelers spend no more than eight hours per day on the river, except for the Part 1 seven-day oar exception.
All complete legal routes for one type are equally likely in Parts 2 and 3.
A campsite-day collision probability around 0.05 is treated as negligible.
Y=150 is a representative worked campsite count.
Exclusive campsite orbits can decouple trip types without losing the best schedule.
Startup forgone loss is small enough to ignore in seasonal capacity.
Sparse skeleton campsites guarantee all adjacent moves in an orbit are reachable.
Trip route choices can be combined through inclusion-exclusion or the so-called Jordan Formula.
All currently feasible trip types are equally likely choices in Part 3.

results_trace.summary: Part 1 retains twenty-five distinct types only by allowing the seven-day oar type above the eight-hour limit.
The printed two-day cycle contains twenty-six launches and extrapolates to 2340 seasonal launches.
The Part 2 greedy calendar reports 500 launches for Y=150 and threshold 0.05.
A mechanical recount of the displayed Part 2 calendar equals 500.
Eight Part 3 runs are 482, 486, 493, 493, 476, 474, 485, and 475, with mean 483.
Aggregated Part 3 counts total 3864, split 67.7 percent oar and 32.3 percent motor.
First-type sensitivity ranges from 473 to 500, with type 22 producing 500.
Daily-hour sensitivity is 454, 484, 560, 483, and 488 for 7 through 9 hours.
Threshold sensitivity is 215, 376, and 500 for 0.01, 0.025, and 0.05.
The conclusion promotes 2340, 500, and the sample maximum 493 as the three carrying capacities.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The three-regime framing gives judges a clear tradeoff structure when scope and feasibility stay explicit.
A complete concrete schedule is persuasive because it can be replayed, but hard travel and horizon violations undermine the headline count.
Sensitivity tables can build trust only when contradictory runs such as 560 versus 500 are investigated rather than described as stable.

weaknesses.summary: Carrying capacity is defined as trip count rather than passengers, vessel occupancy, ecological pressure, or total person-days.
The claim that three capacities must decline only because control is relaxed is not a controlled comparison because the type set and risk semantics also change.
Campsites are numbered 0 through Y+1 although only Y campsites are stated; launch and exit endpoints are not cleanly distinguished from campsites.
The daily travel assumption calls half a day eight hours and later alternates among at most, less than, and deliberately above eight hours.
The assumption lists both 0.05 and 0.025 without assigning them to models or risk meanings.
A local campsite-day probability below 0.05 does not control the probability of any collision across 150 campsites, 180 launch days, or the full network.
Y=150, uniform campsite spacing, and the 225-mile Grand Canyon analogy lack a traceable calibrated data source.
The seven-day oar type requires 225/(4*7)=8.0357 hours per day; printing 8.03 and adding it back violates the stated hard limit.
The printed 8.03 is truncated; ordinary two-decimal rounding gives 8.04.
Twenty-five residue classes do not all contain exactly Y/25 campsites unless Y is divisible by 25.
The orbit-spacing approximation uses 225/Y even though Y internal campsites between two endpoints imply Y+1 intervals.
The integer variables z_i lack a declared domain, solver, existence proof, and reproducible construction.
Filling positions ahead of a leader does not by itself prove optimality through startup, steady state, termination, and season boundaries.
Chart 3 uses six campsite nights for a seven-day type, exposing an unresolved days-versus-nights convention.
The formula m_i=floor(180 n_i/d_i) conflicts with route tables that occupy d_i-1 internal campsites and with the M-6 launch frequency.
Trip-count ratios do not equal orbit-size ratios when durations differ unless duration weights are retained.
Ignoring forgone loss supports an approximation, not an exact best-schedule proof.
The paper prints min A_i=A_3 although the retained seven-day oar type has the largest daily-hour requirement.
The paper prints A_i>=A_3 where the feasibility ordering requires A_i<=A_3.
The seven-point skeleton formulas do not specify rounding for noninteger fractions and contain a visibly malformed k range.
The threshold 306 sums durations, while the later Y=150 construction uses duration minus one; the campsite requirement is inconsistent.
The threshold 149 is arithmetically correct but adopts a different campsite-night convention from the 306 threshold.
Replacing 7,7,8 by arbitrary combinations does not prove daily travel or collision feasibility for every requested ratio.
The claim of uniform type distribution is contradicted by motorized six-day trips launching on both days of the cycle.
Twenty-five distinct feasible types produce twenty-six launches per two-day cycle because M-6 is duplicated; the prose risks conflating types and launches.
Chart 7 leaves campsite 150 unused and averages about 143 of 150 occupied campsites per cycle, contrary to full-utilization rhetoric.
Several printed oar routes require roughly nine to ten-and-a-half hours in a day, so the 2340 schedule violates the travel constraint beyond the O-7 average.
The 2340 arithmetic permits long trips launched on day 180 to finish after the six-month horizon; an in-season completion interpretation gives a lower count.
The table explanation alternates between day and night terminology and gives an example multiplicity that is not visible in the cited row.
The sequence n through n+m contains m+1 types; an m-type group should end at n+m-1.
The Y<18 boundary conflicts with the paper's use of d-1 internal campsite nights.
The jump from two and three types to arbitrary groups has no invariant, feasibility proof, or optimality proof.
The inclusion-exclusion final term visibly repeats the union; the standard formula requires the intersection of all n events.
Calling inclusion-exclusion Jordan Formula does not define the event family, dependence assumptions, or the probability of at least two occupancies.
The text alternates between below 0.05 and probability 0.05 being treated as impossible, leaving equality ambiguous.
The recursion defines x only through Y but the occupancy formula uses f(T,Y+1,duration).
The printed occupancy probability uses a suffix count at the full duration rather than remaining time d-t and can fail probability normalization.
The paper declares only twenty-four legal types but continues to write candidate domains 1 through 26 without an implementation-level filter.
The greedy minimax schedule is a local heuristic and has no exchange argument, upper bound, exact comparison, or global-optimum proof.
The q function is never given an explicit computable formula and independence among trip route choices is not stated.
An arbitrary set of X given trips may already violate the collision threshold or may not correspond to a prefix of the greedy construction.
Multiple fixed-route given trips can collide deterministically; the continuation procedure does not state a feasibility rejection step.
Part 3 samples a feasible type for each launch rather than modeling tourists choosing types after launch, so the stochastic interface does not match the claimed freedom.
Random feasible selection has no seeds, tie policy, run-count justification, convergence diagnostic, or optimality guarantee.
The eight capacities have mean 483 and range 474-493; selecting the repeated maximum 493 is post-selection, not a representative or proven optimum.
Chart 12 aggregates all eight runs rather than documenting the complete schedule for either 493 realization.
Uniform selection from a changing feasible set produces a highly skewed final type distribution and is not equivalent to uniform overall type demand.
Chart 13 ranges from 473 to 500, so the first trip has a material effect and the main 500 is the maximum case.
Chart 14 visually confirms 454, 484, 560, 483, 488; the isolated 560 contradicts Chart 13, Chart 15, and the 500 main result under the stated same baseline.
The nonmonotone daily-hours sweep cannot support the claim that results change only slightly.
Changing the small-probability threshold from 0.025 to 0.05 changes capacity from 376 to 500, so the two values cannot be treated interchangeably.
Equal complete-route probabilities and equal feasible-type selection are admitted simplifications that directly determine the reported capacities.
Repeated use of optimal for the orbit construction, greedy schedule, and random maximum exceeds the evidence supplied.
References 2 and 3 are visually identical, the first source is a weak question-answer page, and reference-to-assumption linkage is missing.
No code, random seeds, machine-readable schedules, probability checks, or complete reproduction package is supplied.
The manager letter repeats 2340, 500, and 493 without carrying the hard-constraint failures and uncertainty needed for a decision.
The manager letter prints separate 'which' where the intended term is orbits.
Internal headers show page 21 of 20 and page 22 of 20; the denominator was not updated for the letter.
The final three lines are stranded on an otherwise almost empty page, creating an avoidable orphan and pagination defect.

independent_extensions.summary: Replace uniform campsite spacing and web analogies with surveyed campsite coordinates, closures, capacities, ecological limits, and trip demand.
Enforce daily travel and season-end constraints exactly, with explicit day-versus-night indexing and no near-threshold exceptions.
Formulate fixed-route scheduling as a time-expanded conflict graph or integer program and compare orbit cycles with exact upper bounds.
Correct the prefix-suffix probability with remaining time, define q explicitly, test normalization, and validate collision risk by simulation.
Control system-wide collision probability through a union bound, chance constraint, or target expected collision count rather than per-cell 0.05.
Model tourist type choice with an estimated mixed distribution and optimize offered departures before choices are realized.
Use frozen code, seeds, many independent runs, mean and quantile reporting, and exact small-instance benchmarks.
Investigate and reconcile the 560 spike before drawing any sensitivity conclusion.

candidate_rule_impacts.action: retain three-regime framing, orbit-to-cycle exposition, probability dataflow, sensitivity interpretation, and manager-letter translation with explicit scope
retain the context-to-definitions-to-assumptions-to-controlled schedule-to-probabilistic schedule-to-random comparator-to-sensitivity-to-decision chain
treat campsite coordinates, trip types, route tables, calendar entries, route probabilities, random seeds, and sensitivity settings as versioned data
maintain an assumption ledger for spacing, daily travel, day-night indexing, route choice, type choice, local risk, and season boundaries
retain orbit partition, cyclic scheduling, dynamic route counting, collision aggregation, greedy insertion, and random construction only with typed interfaces
combine trip count, person-days, campsite use, daily travel, route freedom, local and global collision risk, mix balance, and operating horizon in one decision rule
keep arithmetic launch counts, replayed feasibility, greedy best observed, random sample maximum, and proven optimum separately labeled
stress Y, spacing, hours, duration indexing, probability threshold, route distribution, first type, season end, and random seed
make reliability route-replay-, normalization-, network-risk-, seed-, sample-, bound-, and horizon-specific
reconcile 25 versus 26, days versus nights, union versus intersection, remaining time, 500 versus 560, and 483 versus 493 before reuse
retain charts only with route timing, table headers, continuation semantics, exact totals, parameter settings, and linked contradictions
choose dynamic programming, incremental probability updates, exact scheduling, random multi-run evaluation, caching, runtime, and memory strategies from measured problem size
